title: That Dang-old Goat Fell Over
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss fainting goats (myotonic goats, Tennessee fainting goats, Tennessee stiff legs, wooden legs). They trace the goat's association with Satanism from the Mendesian goat worship described by Herodotus, the Greek god Pan, and the Baphomet image linked to the Knights Templar and the nineteenth-century Eliphas Levi drawing. They explain myotonia congenita as a congenital muscle stiffness caused by a chloride channel (CLCN1) gene problem, compare it to the hypnic jerk and myoclonus, and cover the history of the breed from John Tinsley bringing goats from Nova Scotia to Marshall County, Tennessee in the 1880s, its breeding for meat and novelty, the sacrificial-lamb idea, and artificial selection. A listener email from Ed in Chico, California, a crime scene investigator, follows and corrects TV portrayals of forensic work.

segments.title: Opening banter and the goat as Satanic symbol
segments.summary: Hosts open with small talk about Chuck feeling sick, then discuss how the goat became associated with Satanism, tracing it from Herodotus's account of Mendesian goat worship and the Greek god Pan to the Baphomet image and the Knights Templar.

segments.title: Fainting goat videos and names
segments.summary: Hosts describe YouTube videos of fainting goats and fainting kittens and list alternate names such as Tennessee stiff legs, wooden legs, and nervous goats.

segments.title: What myotonia congenita is
segments.summary: The hosts explain that fainting is actually a congenital muscle condition, myotonia congenita, in which muscles tense up and take ten to twenty seconds to relax, rather than a startle response that causes fainting. They note the condition also occurs in humans, at about one in 100,000 people overall and one in 10,000 in northern Scandinavia.

segments.title: Hypnic jerk and the chloride gene mechanism
segments.summary: The hosts compare myotonia to myoclonus and the hypnic jerk, then explain that the condition comes from a CLCN1 chloride channel gene problem, leaving too much sodium relative to chloride so muscles take longer to relax. It can be inherited dominantly or recessively.

segments.title: Breeding history and uses of fainting goats
segments.summary: The hosts describe how fainting goats were bred for meat and novelty, and how John Tinsley reportedly brought them from Nova Scotia to Marshall County, Tennessee in the 1880s. The breed became established by the 1950s and spread to Texas, and by the 1980s it had split into meat and novelty lines. Younger goats fall more often.

segments.title: Sacrificial lamb idea and artificial selection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the theory that farmers kept fainting goats with herds as sacrificial animals to distract predators, noting there is little evidence for it. They frame the breeding as artificial selection, a trait that natural selection would remove, and mention the animal welfare groups PETA and the Humane Society.

segments.title: Breed status and conservation
segments.summary: The hosts report that fainting goats are recognized as a separate American breed, with about three thousand to five thousand animals, and that The Livestock Conservancy recommends protecting the breed.

segments.title: Personal goat anecdotes
segments.summary: Chuck describes his pet goats, including Nestor, and Josh recounts meeting a baby goat at a Santa Barbara winery. The hosts joke about goats and kittens.

segments.title: Wrap-up and listener email
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck recap the topics and point listeners to the HowStuffWorks article on fainting goats. They then read a listener email from Ed in Chico, California, a crime scene investigator who says TV forensics misrepresents how long DNA and latent print analysis takes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and invite listeners to email about artificial selection and to follow the show on social media.
